findings.who: An employee who got tips from one employer for two jobs, only one of them on the list. For example, a restaurant shift manager (not listed) who also works shifts as a server or bartender (listed), or a hotel front-desk clerk who also works as a bellhop.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether 'the work you got these tips for' is on the list. That work as a whole is not, so a truthful answer is no. The help confirms the no: 'If the work is not on it, tips from this employer cannot be deducted.' The question offers no 'partly' answer.
findings.line: tipjob.other_work_if_listed (the refusal is missed) and tipjob.amount (the listed-occupation tips are silently zeroed)
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 103: 'If you received tips as an employee in more than one occupation for the same employer, only those tips that were received in an occupation on the list ... are considered qualified tips.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'Did you get any of these tips while working in a job on the IRS list?' (Yes covers partly.) Then ask tipjob.other_work after a yes. Change the help to: 'If none of the work you got tips for is on the list...'

findings.who: An employee whose listed occupation is not among the gate's examples: a cook, dishwasher or baker sharing in a tip pool; a casino dealer; a musician; a valet; a nanny; a massage therapist; a tattoo artist; a golf caddy; a home mover; a tutor; a locksmith; a pet caretaker; a fitness instructor.
findings.why_no: The gate names 'Restaurant, bar and hotel staff, hairdressers and barbers, and taxi and delivery drivers.' A filer who does not visit the URL reads this as the list. 'Customarily get tips' also invites the filer's own judgment, for example that cooks or dishwashers do not customarily get tips.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 103: 'Beverage and food service: ... chefs and cooks (105); dishwashers (108) ... Entertainment and events: gambling dealers (201) ... musicians and singers (206) ... Personal services: ... tutors (507), and nannies and babysitters (508) ... Transportation and delivery: parking and valet attendants (801) ... home movers (809).'
findings.fix: Show the full set of category headings with examples from p. 103 (beverage and food service including cooks and dishwashers; entertainment and casino; hospitality; home services; personal services; personal appearance and wellness; recreation and instruction; transportation and delivery). Say: 'These are examples only. Check the full list before answering no.'

findings.who: An employee whose job title differs from the list's occupation titles: a barista, busser, food runner, barback, sommelier, nail technician, esthetician, shampoo assistant, room-service attendant or casino cocktail server.
findings.why_no: The filer searches the list for their own job title, does not find it, and answers no. They are actually covered by an occupation description or illustrative example (for example wait staff, bartenders, or barbers, hairdressers, hairstylists and cosmetologists 603).
findings.irs_text: i1040gi pp. 102-103: the list 'provides for each occupation ... an occupation title, a description of the types of services performed ... illustrative examples of specific occupations that would be included, and the ... SOC system code(s)'.
findings.fix: Tell the filer to match the duties they performed against the occupation descriptions and illustrative examples, not their job title. Better: ask what work they did and map it to a TTOC code in the tool.

findings.who: An employee in a listed occupation working for an employer outside restaurants, bars and hotels: a bartender or server at a country club, stadium, hospital or catering company; a valet employed by a hospital; a hairstylist at a spa; a delivery driver for a grocery chain.
findings.why_no: The examples name industries ('Restaurant, bar and hotel staff'). A filer whose employer is not a restaurant, bar or hotel concludes the work is not on the list, even though the list is by occupation.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 102: 'it must have been paid to you while you were working in an occupation that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024.'
findings.fix: Say that the list is of occupations, not employers: 'It is your job duties that count, whatever kind of business employs you.'

findings.who: A joint filer completing the tipjob document for the spouse's W-2 from a tipped job, where the filer has no tipped work.
findings.why_no: 'Is the work you got these tips for' is read as the filer's own work, so the filer answers no for the spouse's employer.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 101: 'You (and/or your spouse if filing a joint return) received qualified tips in 2025.'
findings.fix: Name the person whose W-2 this is in the question: 'Is the work [name] got these tips for...'
